reason: A five-word run made entirely of a genitive and a conjunction. Judges 1:33 is Naphtali failing to drive out the Canaanites; Helaman 3:7 is a timber shortage answered by cement. The only content word shared is 'land', and the Book of Mormon's 'upon the face of the land, nevertheless the people which went forth' is its own standing construction.

sharedText: the face of the whole earth
reason: Worth writing out because the pull is toward Babel and Hardy's apparatus does cross-reference Genesis 11:4 elsewhere in this book, at Helaman 6:28. “the face of the whole earth” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, and in Genesis 11 the phrase is twice the *punishment* — the builders say 'lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth' and the LORD scatters them upon it. Helaman 3:8 has the Nephites 'begin to cover the face of the whole earth' as a blessing of increase, in a verse whose other half is the fourfold sea formula and whose sense is Genesis 1:28's replenishing, not Genesis 11's dispersal. The senses are opposed at the one point that matters: Babel's spreading is a judgment on a people who wanted to stay together, and this one is prosperity.

'The church of God' occurs across Acts, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians and 1 Timothy and is the New Testament's ordinary name for the body; the Book of Mormon uses it in the same ordinary way here and at 3:33. 1 Corinthians 10:32 is an instruction about giving no offence to Jews, Gentiles or the church, which has no bearing on a mass baptism. Covers the same candidate at 3:33.

A five-word run in which four words are function words and the fifth is the divine name. Psalm 34:8's clause is 'O taste and see that the LORD is good' — an invitation to try him; Helaman 3:27's is 'Thus we may see that the Lord is merciful unto all who will … call upon his holy name' — a conclusion drawn from a narrative. 'Thus we see' is Mormon's own editorial formula, used three times in four verses here (3:27, 3:28, 3:29), and it is what generates the match.

“in the fiftieth year” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it ranked second in the chapter, and the singleton is arithmetic rather than diction: the KJV dates by regnal year constantly and had occasion to write 'fiftieth' once, in Pekahiah's accession notice. Helaman 3:32 is counting the reign of the judges. See the standing entry at Helaman 1:1, which covers every dating candidate in these chapters.

A five-word run of a phrase the KJV uses wherever a population's morale or disposition is in question, and which the Book of Mormon uses constantly. Joshua 7:5's hearts melt and become as water after the defeat at Ai; Helaman 3:33's receive pride. Covers the same candidate at 3:36.

A tempting place to reach for the New Testament's affliction vocabulary — 'the more humble part of the people to suffer great persecutions, and to wade through much affliction' — and there is nothing to reach for. The Book of Mormon's verb is 'wade', which does not occur in the King James Bible at all: the KJV's water-crossing verbs are 'pass over' and 'go through', and wading through affliction is nineteenth-century English rather than King James English. 2 Corinthians 4:17's 'light affliction, which is but for a moment' shares the noun and nothing else, and its argument (affliction working an eternal weight of glory) is not this verse's (pride in the church persecuting the humble). Recorded because the clause reads biblical and is not, which is the opposite of what this catalogue usually finds and worth a reader knowing.
